pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** How switches work

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'recognise that a switch opens and closes a circuit and associate this with whether or not a lamp lights in a simple series circuit.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation; 4-PS3-2 foreshadowed only. UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children learn that a switch works by opening and closing the circuit: closed = complete loop = component on; open = break in the loop = component off. The idea is purely topological (make/break the path), not about how a switch is engineered. The switch is the deliberate, controllable version of the 'break in the loop' children meet in 'will it light?': it makes the complete-loop rule into something they operate on purpose.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Connect the switch directly to the complete-loop rule already met: a switch is just a gap you can open and close on demand — closed completes the loop, open breaks it.
Let children make a switch from everyday materials (two drawing pins and a paperclip, or two foil tabs) so they SEE that closing simply bridges a gap with a conductor.
Use predict-then-test: 'switch open — will the lamp light?' before flipping, so the open/closed ↔ off/on mapping is committed and checked.
Place the switch at different points in the loop to show position doesn't matter — a break anywhere stops the whole series circuit (foreshadows series behaviour without theorising).
Name the two states precisely and consistently — OPEN (broken, off) and CLOSED (complete, on) — because the everyday meaning of 'open' (as in 'open for business/on') fights the technical one.
keyRepresentations: A simple gap-switch: two contacts and a conductive bridge (paperclip/foil) that physically closes the gap.
The same circuit shown twice — switch open (red break, lamp dark) and switch closed (green loop, lamp lit).
The conventional switch symbol shown in both open and closed positions as a label for the handled object.
A finger-trace loop that is interrupted at the switch when open and continuous when closed.
commonMisconceptions: Reversing the words: assuming 'open' means on/working (everyday 'open') when electrically open means broken/off.
Thinking the switch generates or adds power rather than simply completing or breaking an existing loop.
Believing a switch must sit right next to the bulb or the battery to work, rather than anywhere in the loop.
Carrying over the unipolar idea — that the switch only needs to connect 'one side' — rather than completing the whole path.
Thinking flicking a switch changes how much electricity flows (dimmer/brighter) rather than simply on/off at this level.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach that a switch is simply a gap in the circuit loop that you can open and close on purpose: closed = complete loop = component on; open = break in the loop = component off. Children build and operate switches from everyday materials, use predict-then-test, and move the switch to different loop positions to see that a break anywhere stops the whole series circuit. The key conceptual hurdle is naming the states correctly against the everyday meaning of 'open'. Aligned to UK DfE KS2 Year 4 Electricity.

activities.title: Operate a switch and name OPEN/CLOSED against intuition
feedback: If a learner says 'open' should mean on, point to the visible gap: an open gap breaks the loop so no current can go all the way round — the lamp is off. Contrast with the everyday word deliberately.
If a learner thinks the switch adds or makes power, highlight that the cell is the energy source; the switch only completes or breaks the path — the lamp cannot light unless the whole loop is closed.
Reinforce by tracing the loop with a finger: continuous (green) when closed, interrupted at the switch (red break) when open.
activities.rationale: Letting children operate the make/break themselves and commit a prediction before checking is intended to cement the open/closed ↔ off/on mapping, which children most often reverse because of the everyday meaning of 'open'. An on-screen model with a live-path highlight that breaks at the switch, or a physical gap-switch, both make the mechanism visible.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement: recognise that a switch opens and closes a circuit and associate this with whether a lamp lights.
Children frequently reverse open/closed and carry unipolar ideas to switches; building a switch as a bridgeable gap and predict-then-test address this.
learnerActions: Work with a circuit (physical or on-screen model) and tap or flick the switch to open and close it.

Watch the contact bridge the gap when closed — the loop completes and the lamp glows — and lift when open, leaving a visible break exactly at the switch so the lamp dies. On an on-screen model this can be shown with the completed loop highlighted green and the break drawn in red at the switch.
Say out loud the correct name for each state: OPEN means the gap is open, so the circuit is broken and the lamp is OFF; CLOSED means the gap is closed, so the loop is complete and the lamp is ON.
Predict before each flip: 'switch open — will the lamp light?' then flip and check.
activities.intendedInsight: A switch is just a controllable gap in the loop; OPEN = broken = off, CLOSED = complete = on — the opposite of the everyday sense of 'open' (as in 'open for business').

activities.title: Build your own switch from everyday materials
feedback: If the lamp does not light, check that the bridge actually touches both contacts and that the rest of the loop is complete — a break anywhere stops it.
If a learner thinks only 'one side' needs connecting, show that current must travel all the way round the whole loop; a single contact is not enough.
activities.rationale: Making the switch from familiar materials lets children SEE that closing bridges a gap with a conductor, directly connecting the switch to the complete-loop rule and intended to counter the unipolar (connect-one-side) idea.
sourceClaims: Children frequently reverse open/closed and carry unipolar ideas to switches; building a switch as a bridgeable gap and predict-then-test address this.
learnerActions: Make a switch from two drawing pins and a paperclip, or two foil tabs, placed in a simple series circuit with a cell and a lamp (or buzzer).
Bridge the two contacts with the paperclip (or foil) and observe the lamp light; lift the bridge to break the gap and watch it go out.
Describe in your own words that closing the switch simply bridges a gap with a conductor, completing the loop.
activities.intendedInsight: Closing a switch is nothing more than bridging a gap with a conductor to complete the loop; a switch is a deliberate, controllable version of the 'break in the loop' from earlier circuit work.

activities.title: Move the switch — position doesn't matter
feedback: If a learner expects the switch to work only when next to the bulb, move it to the far side and flick: the lamp still goes off. The loop is a single path, so one gap stops it all.
Connect to home experience: a light switch by the door turns off a bulb on the ceiling because it breaks the loop that bulb is on, not because the switch is near the bulb.
Counterexample to discuss: if a wire falls off far from the switch, the bulb goes out even with the switch CLOSED — because that too breaks the one loop.
activities.rationale: Repositioning the switch and predict-then-test confronts the misconception that a switch must be adjacent to the bulb or battery and foreshadows series behaviour without theorising.
learnerActions: Place (or drag) the switch to three different points around the series loop — near the lamp, near the cell, and on the far side away from both.
Predict each time: will flicking the switch still turn the lamp off, even though it isn't next to the lamp? Then flick to check.
Explain why the switch works from anywhere: a break anywhere in a single series loop stops current everywhere.
activities.intendedInsight: A break anywhere in the loop stops the whole series circuit, so a switch controls the lamp from any position — it need not sit next to the bulb or battery.

activities.title: Check the open↔off, closed↔on mapping
feedback: For a wrong match, return to a worked or operated example and re-trace the loop: open = gap = broken = off.
If a learner says electricity waits or piles up at the open switch, trace the broken loop together — an open gap means no current flows anywhere, so nothing accumulates.
Treat this as a check of the mapping, not where the intuition is first built — pair it with hands-on operation.
activities.rationale: A matching/multiple-choice check can fairly assess the open↔off / closed↔on mapping and switch-position reasoning, and probe the 'electricity stored at the switch' idea, though recognition responses do not on their own elicit the independent construction that operating a real or modelled switch provides.
learnerActions: Match OPEN to off and CLOSED to on, and look at circuit images with the switch in each state to decide whether the lamp lights.
Answer 'which switch position lights the lamp?' and justify why.
When off, consider where the electricity is: trace the broken loop to see that flow stops everywhere and nothing piles up at the switch.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can read a switch's state and predict the lamp result, reinforces the correct vocabulary, and checks that an open loop means no flow anywhere rather than electricity stored at the switch.

constraints: Name the two states precisely and consistently — OPEN (broken, off) and CLOSED (complete, on) — because the everyday meaning of 'open' (on/available) fights the technical one.
Keep the idea topological: a switch makes or breaks the path; it is not about how a switch is engineered.
At this level, a switch is on/off only — avoid suggesting flicking it changes how much electricity flows (dimmer/brighter).
An open loop means no current flows anywhere; electricity is not stored or waiting at the open switch.
Matching/multiple-choice tasks assess the mapping but do not, on their own, build the intuition; pair them with hands-on operation or a manipulable model.
A two-state tap illustration (open vs closed with state labels) is a useful scaffold for fixing vocabulary, but it lacks the learner's own repeated operation that cements the mapping.
When asking learners to predict whether the lamp lights, describe the switch's state clearly so the open/closed ↔ off/on relationship is unambiguous.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (IOP Spark / SPT misconceptions) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its misconception claims as plausible guidance rather than confirmed evidence.

The original claimed dialogue and 3D 'add nothing' for this topic; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts. A conversation can still support reasoning and a physical build is itself three-dimensional — these have been reframed as scaffolding/assessment choices rather than universal limits.
Physical paperclip/foil switches and on-screen models offer different experiences; neither is asserted to be universally necessary or superior.

The DfE statutory claim is cited in activity 1 because it states the open/closed→lamp mapping that is the activity's intended insight; it supports that content/standard, not any particular method's efficacy.

assess.poeTask: Build a series loop with the switch on the far side, away from the bulb. Ask the child to predict — will flicking this switch still turn the bulb off, even though it isn't next to the bulb? Why? The 'switch is a local tap/source' child expects it not to work from a distance; the 'breaks the one loop' child says it works from anywhere. Then flick it to reveal.
probeDeeper: If I put the switch on the OTHER side of the loop, will it still turn the bulb off? Why?
When the switch is open, is there electricity sitting in the wires waiting? How do you know?
Counterexample: a loose wire falls off somewhere far from the switch, and the bulb goes out even though the switch is ON. Why?
A light in your house has a switch by the door but the bulb is on the ceiling. How can a switch so far away turn it off?
assess.correctAnswer: The switch opens a gap in the loop, breaking the complete circuit so current can no longer flow all the way round — so the bulb stops. The electricity isn't stored up or sent away; the flow simply stops everywhere because the loop is broken. Closing the switch mends the loop and current flows again.

errorPatterns.pattern: The switch turns the electricity on and off like a tap, or makes the power ('the switch gives the bulb its electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the cell is the energy source; the switch only closes or opens the loop — move the switch to different places and it still just breaks the loop.
errorPatterns.distractor: The switch turns on the electricity and sends it to the bulb.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the switch as a source or supply rather than a gap in the loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: When off, the electricity waits at the switch, piling up until you turn it on ('it's stored there ready').
errorPatterns.nextMove: An open loop means NO flow anywhere and nothing piles up — trace the broken loop together.
errorPatterns.distractor: When it's off, the electricity waits at the switch until you flick it on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says charge or electricity accumulates at the open switch.

errorPatterns.pattern: A switch has to be right next to the bulb (or the battery) to work ('it only works in one place').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move the switch to different points in the series loop — it controls the bulb from anywhere because it breaks the one loop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Thinks the switch's position in the loop matters for whether it controls the bulb.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the switch as a source or store — it 'makes' or 'holds' the electricity; can't say it opens or closes the loop.
responseLevels.full: Explains the switch makes or breaks the single loop (open = gap = no flow anywhere; closed = complete = current flows), and applies it — the switch works from any point, and any other break stops the bulb too.
responseLevels.partial: Says the switch turns the bulb on and off and that closing it lets current flow, but still talks of electricity being stored at the switch or 'sent', or thinks position matters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you flick a switch OFF, the bulb goes out. Where does the electricity go, and what has the switch actually done to the circuit to make the bulb stop?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the switch is a source or store ('it holds back the electricity' or 'turns the power on') answers differently from one who says it opens/closes a gap in the loop. The reason tier separates 'switch controls a supply' from 'switch makes or breaks the complete loop'.
